The certainty of evidence was downgraded from high to very low because of serious concerns regarding bias, inconsistency, and indirectness. 3. Running at a recreational level was found to have a protective effect against the development of hip and/or knee osteoarthritis (OA). 4. The confounding effects of associated risk factors, such as age, gender, weight, occupational workload, and previous injuries, on the risk of OA in runners could not be demonstrated. 5. Studies included populations of recreational runners and orienteers but did not analyze these groups separately. 6. The heterogeneity between studies was low (I² = 0%), with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 0% to 73%. 7. Based on the available evidence, it is not possible to conclude whether running is associated with an increased risk of knee OA, as the studies provided conflicting results. 8. No dose-response relationship was reported, as this review focused solely on adverse health outcomes related to OA. 9. The meta-analysis combined data from running and orienteering populations but did not analyze these activities separately. 10. The risk of bias was assessed using a tool not specifically designed for observational or etiologic association studies, which may have influenced the findings. 11. Sixteen out of twenty-five studies were rated as having a high risk of bias in their detection methods. 12. Due to high heterogeneity between studies (as indicated by a high I² statistic), a random-effects model was used, which can sometimes disproportionately weight smaller studies. 13. The populations under investigation were not homogeneous, and the outcomes were defined differently across studies. 14. The certainty of evidence was downgraded to very low due to serious concerns about bias, inconsistency, and indirectness. 15. The review considered five outcomes related to knee OA: diagnosis of knee OA, radiographic and imaging markers, knee arthroplasty, knee pain, and knee-associated disability. 16. Due to the heterogeneity in outcome definitions and measurement methods, only one meta-analysis was deemed appropriate, which combined case-control studies identifying knee surgery cases due to OA. 17. Overall, no definitive conclusion could be drawn regarding the relationship between running and knee OA as a long-term adverse health outcome. 18. For erectile dysfunction, the systematic review did not qualify for GRADE evidence assessment due to a critically low rating on the AMSTAR 2 scale. 19. No systematic reviews were found regarding the relationship between exposure to air pollution and adverse health outcomes for assessing GRADE evidence. 20. Studies evaluating the effects of resistance training on sleep outcomes showed mixed results, with some reporting significant improvements in subjective sleep quality and others finding no effect. 21. Exercise interventions lasting at least six weeks were associated with reduced symptoms of insomnia among middle-aged and older women compared to no exercise. 22. Tai Chi interventions in perimenopausal women showed no consistent effects on quality of life measures across all subscales of the SF-36 instrument. 23. A single session of physical activity close to bedtime significantly increased REM latency and slow-wave sleep while decreasing stage 1 sleep, but no effects were observed for other sleep parameters. 24. The association between physical activity and the incidence of hypertension among South Asian adults showed mixed results, with some studies reporting lower odds of hypertension with moderate physical activity and others finding no association. 25. The certainty of evidence was downgraded due to serious concerns about bias, inconsistency, indirectness, and imprecision in the studies reviewed. 26. The WHO guideline development group used a PECO (Population-Exposure-Control-Outcome) framework to define the scope of their guidelines, focusing on critical and important health outcomes such as all-cause mortality, type 2 diabetes, cancer, osteoarthritis, mental health outcomes, body weight, cognitive outcomes, sleep quality, hypertension, and health-related quality of life. 27. Systematic searches for relevant evidence were conducted in December 2019 across multiple databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and SportDiscus, without restrictions on publication date. 28. The search strategy included keywords such as occupational physical activity, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses, and the results were exported into a reference manager for further analysis.
